lessons.title: Greetings and Introductions
lessons.body: In Swahili, greetings are more than just wordsâthey are the key to opening doors in East Africa. Whether you are in Nairobi, Dar es Salaam, or Kampala, starting with a proper greeting shows respect and builds trust. The most common greeting is "Jambo!" which means "Hello!" but it is often used with tourists. For a more authentic feel, use "Habari?" (How are you?) and respond with "Nzuri" (Good) or "Salama" (Peaceful). Another essential is "Shikamoo" to elders, meaning "I hold your feet" as a sign of respect; the elder replies "Marahaba." For peers, "Mambo?" (What's up?) and "Poa" (Cool) are popular among youth. When introducing yourself, say "Jina langu ni..." (My name is...). To ask someone's name, say "Jina lako ni nani?" If you want to know where someone is from, ask "Unatoka wapi?" and answer with "Natoka..." followed by your country. For example, "Natoka Kenya." Practice these with a partner: greet, ask name, ask origin, and say goodbye with "Kwaheri" (Goodbye) or "Tutaonana" (See you later). In business settings, always greet before stating your purpose. A handshake is common, but wait for a woman to extend her hand first. In rural areas, you might be greeted with "Hujambo?" (Are you fine?) and you reply "Sijambo" (I am fine). Remember, taking time to greet properly is never wasted; it is an investment in relationships. Try using these phrases daily with Swahili speakers you meet, and you will quickly see smiles and doors open.

lessons.title: The Swahili Alphabet and Pronunciation
lessons.body: Swahili uses the Latin alphabet, but with a few tweaks. There are 26 letters, but some are pronounced differently than in English. The good news: Swahili is phoneticâevery letter is pronounced exactly as it is written. Vowels are pure and short: a (ah), e (eh), i (ee), o (oh), u (oo). So "mama" is mah-mah, not may-may. Consonants are mostly like English, but watch out for these: 'g' is always hard as in "go," never soft; 'j' is pronounced like the 'j' in "jump"; 'ch' is like 'ch' in "church"; 'ny' is like the 'ny' in "canyon"; and 'ng' at the beginning of a word is like the 'ng' in "sing" but with a hard 'g' soundâpractice saying "ng'ombe" (cow). The letter 'r' is rolled slightly, similar to Spanish. There are no silent letters. Stress usually falls on the second-to-last syllable: "ki-TA-bu" (book), "ha-BA-ri" (news). To practice, say these words aloud: "asante" (thank you), "karibu" (welcome), "safari" (journey), "lala" (sleep). A common mistake is to pronounce vowels as diphthongs; keep them short and crisp. For example, "bei" (price) is beh-ee, not bay. Listen to Swahili radio or music to train your ear. Try recording yourself and compare with native speakers. With consistent practice, you'll master the sounds quickly.

lessons.title: Basic Numbers 1-10
lessons.body: Numbers are essential for shopping, bargaining, and telling time. In Swahili, numbers 1 to 10 are straightforward. Here they are: 1 - moja, 2 - mbili, 3 - tatu, 4 - nne, 5 - tano, 6 - sita, 7 - saba, 8 - nane, 9 - tisa, 10 - kumi. Notice that 'moja' starts with 'm', and 'mbili' has a slight hum at the startâpractice saying 'm' and 'b' together. When counting objects, you use different prefixes depending on the noun class, but for now, just learn the basic forms. To say "one book," you say "kitabu kimoja" (ki- prefix for kitabu). But for numbers above one, the number itself often stays the same: "vitabu vitatu" (three books). For money, you'll hear "shilingi moja" (one shilling) or "shilingi kumi" (ten shillings). In markets, knowing numbers helps you bargain: "Bei gani?" (What's the price?) Answer might be "shilingi elfu tano" (five thousand shillings). Practice counting out loud daily: moja, mbili, tatu... up to kumi. Then count backwards. Also learn to ask "Una miaka mingapi?" (How old are you?) and answer "Nina miaka ishirini" (I am twenty years old). For phone numbers, you'll hear digits read individually. So a number like 0712 345 678 is read: sifuri saba moja mbili, tatu nne tano, sita saba nane. (Note: 0 is 'sifuri'.) Use these numbers in real situations: buy vegetables, ask for bus fare, or tell your age. Repetition is key.

lessons.title: Common Polite Expressions
lessons.body: Politeness is highly valued in Swahili culture. Using the right expressions shows respect and opens hearts. Start with "Tafadhali" (Please) and "Asante" (Thank you). If someone helps you, say "Asante sana" (Thank you very much). The response is "Karibu" (You're welcome) or "Hakuna matata" (No problem). When you need to interrupt or get attention, say "Samahani" (Excuse me/Sorry). If you accidentally bump someone, "Samahani" works, but for a more sincere apology, say "Nisamehe" (Forgive me). To say "I'm sorry" for a mistake, use "Pole" (pronounced po-leh) when someone is in trouble or has had a misfortune; it means "Sorry" in a sympathetic way. For example, if someone trips, you say "Pole." When leaving, "Kwaheri" (Goodbye) is standard, but "Tutaonana" (See you later) is friendlier. To say "Good morning," use "Habari ya asubuhi?" (News of the morning?) and reply "Nzuri" (Good). In the evening, "Habari ya jioni?" For a polite request, start with "Naomba..." (I request...). For example, "Naomba maji" (I request water). To say "You're welcome" after thanks, you can also say "Karibu tena" (Welcome again). When someone says "Asante" for a gift, you say "Karibu" or "Bila shaka" (Of course). Practice these in daily interactions: at the market, in a matatu, at a restaurant. A simple "Tafadhali" and "Asante" will make people smile and treat you warmly. Remember, tone mattersâspeak softly and sincerely.

lessons.title: Self-Introduction: Name and Origin
lessons.body: Introducing yourself confidently is the first step to making friends in Swahili. Start with a greeting: "Jambo!" or "Habari!" Then say "Jina langu ni..." (My name is...). For example, "Jina langu ni Amina." To ask someone's name, say "Jina lako ni nani?" (What is your name?). If you want to be more formal, "Unaitwa nani?" (What are you called?). After they answer, you can say "Nimefurahi kukutana nawe" (I am happy to meet you). Next, share where you are from: "Natoka..." (I come from...). For example, "Natoka Nigeria" or "Natoka Tanzania." To ask "Where are you from?" say "Unatoka wapi?" If you want to know where someone lives, ask "Unaishi wapi?" (Where do you live?) and answer "Ninaishi..." (I live in...). You can also mention your profession: "Mimi ni mwalimu" (I am a teacher) or "Mimi ni mwanafunzi" (I am a student). To ask about someone's work, say "Unafanya kazi gani?" (What work do you do?). A full introduction might sound like: "Habari! Jina langu ni John. Natoka Uganda. Mimi ni mhandisi. Nimefurahi kukutana nawe." Practice this with a friend, swapping roles. In business settings, you might add your company: "Ninafanya kazi katika kampuni ya..." (I work at ... company). Remember to use "na" for "and" and "lakini" for "but" as you expand. Also, note that in Swahili, the verb comes with the subject prefix, so "natoka" means "I come from," "unatoka" means "you come from." Practice by recording yourself and listening for fluency. Soon, you'll introduce yourself like a native.

lessons.title: Cultural Tips: Greeting Etiquette
lessons.body: Greeting etiquette in Swahili culture is rich and varies across regions. In East Africa, greetings are not rushed; they are a ritual that shows respect and builds community. Always greet before asking for anything. A common sequence: "Shikamoo" to an elder, who replies "Marahaba." Then "Habari yako?" (How are you?) and reply "Nzuri." For peers, "Mambo?" and "Poa." Handshakes are common, but in some Muslim areas, men and women do not shake hands; instead, a woman may place her hand on her chest and nod. In rural areas, you might see people bow slightly. When greeting a group, greet each person individually, starting with the eldest. If you are eating, greet those present but don't interrupt a meal; wait until they finish. In business, a handshake is appropriate, but always greet everyone in the room before sitting. Titles matter: use "Bwana" (Mr.) or "Bi" (Ms.) before a surname. For elders, "Mzee" (elder) or "Mama" (mother) is respectful. When someone greets you, respond warmly and ask about their family: "Habari ya familia?" (How is the family?). This shows you care. If you are visiting a home, bring a small gift and greet everyone. In Swahili, there is a saying: "Mtoto umleavyo ndivyo akuavyo" (As you raise a child, so they grow). Greeting is part of raising respectful children. Also, avoid using left hand to give or receive items; use right hand or both. When leaving, say "Kwaheri" to each person. These small gestures go a long way. Practice with locals, and they will appreciate your effort.

quiz.q: What is the most common Swahili greeting for 'Hello'?
quiz.explanation: Jambo is widely used as a basic hello, though Habari is also common.

quiz.q: How do you respond to 'Shikamoo'?
quiz.explanation: Marahaba is the respectful reply to Shikamoo.

quiz.q: What does 'Jina langu ni...' mean?
quiz.explanation: Jina langu ni translates to 'My name is...'.

quiz.q: How do you ask 'Where are you from?' in Swahili?
quiz.explanation: Unatoka wapi? asks about origin.

quiz.q: Which of these is a polite way to say goodbye?
quiz.explanation: Kwaheri means goodbye.

quiz.q: How is the letter 'a' pronounced in Swahili?
quiz.explanation: Swahili vowels are pure; 'a' is pronounced as 'ah'.

quiz.q: Which letter combination is pronounced like 'ny' in canyon?
quiz.explanation: 'ny' is a distinct sound in Swahili, similar to the 'ny' in canyon.

quiz.q: Where does stress usually fall in Swahili words?
quiz.explanation: Stress typically falls on the penultimate (second-to-last) syllable.

quiz.q: How do you say 'book' in Swahili?
quiz.explanation: Kitabu means book.

quiz.q: Which of these is NOT a Swahili vowel?
quiz.explanation: All are vowels; the question is tricky, but 'o' is a vowel. Actually, all are vowels, so question is invalid. Let's change: Which is a consonant? Options: a, e, i, o, u. But that would be none. Better: Which letter is pronounced like 'ch' in church? Options: ch, sh, th, ng. Answer: ch. So change question 10.

quiz.q: Which letter is pronounced like 'ch' in 'church'?
quiz.explanation: In Swahili, 'ch' is pronounced as in 'church'.

quiz.q: What is the Swahili word for 'one'?
quiz.explanation: Moja means one.

quiz.q: How do you say 'five' in Swahili?
quiz.explanation: Tano means five.

quiz.q: What is the number 'kumi'?
quiz.explanation: Kumi is ten.

quiz.q: How do you say 'three books' in Swahili?
quiz.explanation: Vitabu vitatu means three books, with noun class agreement.

quiz.q: What is the Swahili word for 'zero'?
quiz.explanation: Sifuri means zero.

quiz.q: How do you say 'Please' in Swahili?
quiz.explanation: Tafadhali means please.

quiz.q: What is the response to 'Asante'?
quiz.explanation: Karibu means you're welcome.

quiz.q: What does 'Samahani' mean?
quiz.explanation: Samahani is used to apologize or get attention.

quiz.q: When would you say 'Pole'?
options: B) When someone is in trouble or has a misfortune
quiz.explanation: Pole expresses sympathy or condolence.

quiz.q: How do you say 'Good morning' in Swahili?
quiz.explanation: Habari ya asubuhi? means 'Good morning'.

quiz.q: What does 'Naomba' mean?
quiz.explanation: Naomba is used to make a polite request.

quiz.q: How do you say 'My name is Amina' in Swahili?
quiz.explanation: Jina langu ni Amina is the standard way.

quiz.q: What does 'Nimefurahi kukutana nawe' mean?
options: A) I am happy to meet you
quiz.explanation: It expresses pleasure at meeting someone.

quiz.q: How do you ask 'What work do you do?'
quiz.explanation: Unafanya kazi gani? asks about profession.

quiz.q: What is the Swahili word for 'teacher'?
quiz.explanation: Mwalimu means teacher.

quiz.q: In Swahili culture, what should you do before asking for something?
quiz.explanation: Greeting first is essential etiquette.

quiz.q: How do you greet an elder respectfully?
quiz.explanation: Shikamoo is a sign of respect to elders.

quiz.q: Which hand should you use to give or receive items in Swahili culture?
quiz.explanation: Using the right hand is considered polite.

quiz.q: What does 'Karibu' mean when someone thanks you?
quiz.explanation: Karibu is used as 'you're welcome' after thanks.
